Mosharaf Hossain with Md Nasim Miah with Nazma Afrin. Advocates ------ For the Petitioner in both writ petitions. 
S Rashed Jahangir, DAG with Mahfuza Begum AAG with Nurun Nahar, AAG ------ For the Respondent No. 2 in both writ petitions.

full_judgment:
5. None of the above returns were selected for audit by the NBR in view of the provisions under sub-section (3) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance. However, the Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes (respondent No. 2) initiated proceedings under section 120 of the said Ordinance by issuing notices dated 11-5-2015 under Nothi No. নথি নং (১২০)(৩৭, ৩৮)/কঃঅঃ-৪(চট্টঃ)/রেঞ্জ-১/২০১৪-২০১৫/৭৪২ in Writ Petition No. 7697 of 2015) and under Nothi No. নথি নং (১২০)(৩৩, ৩৪)/কঃঅঃ-৪(চট্টঃ)/রেঞ্জ-১/২০১৪-২০১৫/৭৪০ in Writ Petition No. 7697 of 2015 in order to reassess the income of the petitioners holding that in disposing of the assessments of the petitioners in respect of the said assessment years, the DCT committed various errors as described therein and that such errors caused harm to the revenue. Accordingly, the petitioners were asked to remain present in a hearing to be held on 28-5-2015 at 10-00 am and that, in case of failure of the petitioner to remain present, the said assessments would be disposed of exparte. The petitioner then requested the said Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Tax ("IACT") not to proceed with the said proceedings under section 120 of the said Ordinance, but to no avail. Thereafter, since the petitioners remained absent in the hearing, the said IACT passed the impugned orders dated 28-5-2015 under section 120 of the said Ordinance thereby adding several incomes under sections 30(AA) and 19(3) of the said Ordinance to the earlier disclosed income of the petitioners. Accordingly, by the said impugned orders, direction was given on the DCT to pass revised assessment orders and to issue demands upon the petitioners. Thereupon, the concerned DCT passed the impugned revised assessment orders dated 9-6-2015 determining total income of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 7697 of 2015 at Taka 44,57,95,853 in assessment year 2011-2012 and Taka 45,71,77,614 in assessment year 2012-2013. The DCT also passed revised assessments Orders dated 17-6-2015 determining total incomes of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 7698 of 2015 at Taka 8,47,25,289 in assessment year 2011-2012 and at Taka 9,45,88,836 in assessment year 2012-2013. Being aggrieved by such proceedings under section 120 and the said revised assessment orders, the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rules. At the time of issuance of the Rule, this Court, vide orders dated 27-7-2015, stayed operation of the said impugned orders dated 28-5-2015 (Annexure-C) and revised assessment orders dated 9-6-201 Sand 17-6-2015 (Annexures D and DI) for a period of three months. 

 6. Accordingly, the Rules were taken up for herring by a Division Bench of the High Court Division comprising Mr. Justice Sheikh Hassan Arif and Mr Justice JN Deb Choudhury. In the course of such hearing, the said Division Bench found that there had already been difference of opinion between two Division Benches, namely, the Division Bench presided over by his Lordship Mr Justice AFM Abdur Rahman and the Division Bench presided over by her Ladyship Madam Justice Zinat Ara, on the point whether or not issuance of receipts by the concerned DCT under sub-section (1) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance generates any order of the DCT. In other words, whether the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes (IJCT) [which includes an Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes (IACT) vide sec. 2 (36)] does have any order of the DCT before them in respect of returns submitted under universal self-assessment scheme under section 82BB(1) in order to initiate proceedings under section 120 of the said Ordinance. The said Division Bench then concluded that the Division Benches presided over by his Lordship Mr Justice Rahman [in ITR No. 227 of 2010 (Agrani Insurance Co. vs Commissioner of Taxes) and Reliance Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Taxes, 65 DLR (2013)-426] held that, when the DCT issues such receipt after acceptance of return submitted under section 82BB(1), the said receipt being deemed assessment order under sub-section (1), the IJCT or IACT in fact does not have any order before them to hold the view that the order passed by the DCT is an erroneous order. On the other hand, according to the said Bench, the Bench presided over by Madam Justice Zinat Ara [(Writ Petition No. 1481 of 2014 (Kamal Uddin Ahmed vs Chairman, NBR)] took the view that such deemed assessment through issuance of receipt by the DCT generates an order of the DCT as regards correctness and completeness of the return submitted by the assessee. That means, the said Division Bench presided over by her Ladyship Justice Zinat Ara impliedly held that jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance cannot be debarred on the ground that the IJCT or IACT does not have any order of the DCT before them to find any error therein. In view of above difference on points of law between the said two differently constituted Division Benches, the said Division Bench presided over by Mr Justice Sheikh Hassan Arif, vide order dated 13-12-2015, decided to refer the matters to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constitution of a Full Bench in order to resolve the said difference on points of law. 

 7. Again, in the course of such hearing, the said Division Bench presided over by Mr Justice Sheikh Hassan Arif could not agree with two other differently constituted Division Benches on another point of law decided by the said Division Benches taking the view that the jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance can be invoked on the erroneous order of the DCT only when such error is an error of law and not an error of fact. According to the said Division Bench, a Division Bench presided over by his Lordship Mr Justice AFM Abdur Rahman, in Jamuna Oil Company Limited vs the Commissioner of Taxes (ITR No. 29 of 2010), held that, the jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance can be invoked only on question of error of law and not on error of facts. The same view was expressed, though not specifically relying on any authority, by another Division Bench of this Court presided over by her Ladyship Madam Justice Zinat Ara in an unreported Writ Petition No. 1481 of 2014 (Kamal Uddin Ahmed vs Chairman, NBR). Upon considering the said decisions in Jamuna Oil Case and Kamal Uddin's case as referred to above, the said Division Bench presided over by Mr Justice Sheikh Hassan Arif disagreed with such view mainly on the ground that since the Legislature, under section 120 of the said Ordinance, has clearly mentioned only one qualification for invoking such jurisdiction, namely that the error has to be an error which has direct impact in prejudicial sense on the interest of the revenue, no other qualification can be read therein. Accordingly, on that point of difference, the said Division Bench referred the instant writ petitions to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constituting a Full Bench in 'view of the relevant provisions under Chapter-VII of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (High Court Division) Rules, 1973. Upon reference as aforesaid, the Hon'ble Chief Justice constituted this Full Bench (Larger Bench) comprising Mr Justice Borhanuddin, Mr Justice Sheikh Hassan Arif and Mr Justice JN Deb Choudhury. 

 10. As against above submissions, Mr S Rashed Jahangir, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Department, has drawn this Court's attention of the entire Chapter on the `deeming clause' in the Commentaries of late Mr Mahmudul Islam in his Book "Interpretation of Statutes and Documents" (Mallik Brothers) (2009). Learned DAG then submits that, by `deeming clause', the Legislature creates a legal fiction and the consequence of such legal fiction is that, while interpreting such legal fiction, the Court is obliged to assume all such facts and consequences which are incidental or inevitable corollaries to give effect to such legal fiction. In this connection, learned DAG has further referred to the observation of her Ladyship Justice Zinat Ara in the above cited Kamal Uddin',s case (unreported Writ Petition No. 1481 of 2014) and submits that, issuance of receipt upon accepting the return submitted by an assessee under section 82BB encompasses therein the satisfaction of the DCT as regards the correctness and completeness of such return, and when the DCT is satisfied that the return submitted by the assessee is correct and complete return in view of the provisions of law, he then issues such receipts. Therefore, he submits, in view of such satisfaction of the DCT as well as the deeming clause or legal fiction as created by the Legislature by virtue of the said deeming clause, it cannot be said that issuance of receipt by the DCT does not generate any order of the DCT so that the IJCT or IACT can invoke jurisdiction thereon under section 120 of the said Ordinance. 

 15. Prominent jurists and superior Courts have repeatedly observed that the Legislature is quite competent to create legal fiction by enacting deeming provision for the purpose of assuming the existence of a fact which does not really exist, provided the declaration of non-existent facts as existing does not offend the Constitution (see .IK Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd. vs Union of India, AIR 1988 SC 191, p-202 and Indira Sawhney vs Union of India (2000) 1 SCC 168. The effect of such deeming clause is that the Legislature wants everyone concerned to assume and/or imagine certain facts as existing facts although they are not in real existing, and imagine as real the consequence and incidents which must inevitably have flown from or accompanied it. As for example, if the provision says A is deemed to be B, compliance with A is in law compliance with B and contravention of A is in law contravention of B. 

 17. In another case, namely in CIT Delhi vs S Teja Singh, AIR 1959 SC 352, while dealing with the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, which by section 18-A(3) required any person not hitherto assessed to send in certain circumstances an estimate of his income to the ITO for purposes of advance payment of tax and which by clause (9) provided that if during the course of regular assessment the ITO was satisfied that such person had without reasonable cause failed to comply with clause (3), the assessee 'shall be deemed to have failed to furnish the return of his total income and the provisions of section 28, so far as may be, shall apply accordingly'. The question was whether a penalty could be levied under section 28 which provided for the levy of penalty when a person without reasonable cause failed to furnish a return of his total income after notices under section 22(2) or section 34 had been issued to him. The Supreme Court of India answered the question in the affirmative and held that the failure to send the estimate under clause (3) of section 18-A was, by the fiction created by clause (9) of the same section, deemed to be a failure to send a return and consequently "all those facts on which alone there could be failure to send the return must be deemed to exist and it must accordingly be taken that by reason of this fiction notices required to be given under section 22 must be deemed to have been given", thereby, making section 28 applicable. (See page 355 of the reported case). 

 18. However, the above effect of legal fiction created by the Legislature has some limitations in that the purpose and limit of creation of such fiction has to be determined by the Court. It is the obligation of the Court not only to give effect to the legal fiction as created by the Legislature through deeming provision, but also to apply the said legal fiction in accordance with the purpose for creation of legal fiction and extent of application of such legal fiction. Such view was expressed by Mr Justice SR DAS of Indian Supreme Court in some cases, namely in State of Travancore-Cochin vs Shanmugha Vilas Cashewnut Factory, AIR, 1953 SC 333 and Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. vs State of Bihar, AIR 1955 SC 661. Justice SR Das, in the Bengal Immunity case stated that "legal fictions are created only for some definite purpose" and that "a legal fiction is to be limited to the purpose for which it was created and should not be extended beyond that legitimate field". Same view has been expressed by our Apex Court in Begum BH Syed vs Afzal Jahan, 22 DLR (SC) 8 and Pubali Bank vs Chairman, Labour Court, 44 DLR (AD) 40. 

 19. Keeping the above judicial interpretations and observations in mind, if we examine the legal fiction as created by our Legislature by providing the words "shall be deemed to be an order of assessment" in sub-section (I) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance, it will be clear that though practically no assessment order in the traditional sense is passed by the DCT, or the other authorized official, upon accepting a correct and complete return submitted by and assessee under Universal Self-Assessment Scheme, the DCT or other authorized officer, by issuance of a receipt in favour of the assessee, in fact passes an order declaring that the return submitted by the assessee is a 'correct return' and that it is a 'complete return'. Although, the provisions under sub-section (2) of section 82BB provides for the criteria of complete return in that the return shall be taken to be complete if it is filed in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 75 and tax has been paid in accordance with section 74, the provisions .under section 82BB does not clarify as to what should be the correct return. Again, given that sub-section (2) of section 82BB has provided some guidelines about complete return, still the DCT, or the authorized official has to take a decision as regards completeness of the said return after examining as to whether the said return has been filed in accordance with sub-section (2) of section 75 and as to whether correct tax amount has been paid on the basis of such return in accordance with the provisions under section 74 of the said Ordinance. Only after reaching such satisfaction by the DCT, or the authorized official, that such return is a correct return and a complete return, the DCT is required to issue a receipt in favour of an assessee. When such receipt is issued by the DCT, the said receipt shall be deemed to be an order of assessment for the assessment year for which the said return has been filed. Therefore, though practically no order of assessment in a traditional way is passed by the DCT, or his .authorized officer, it has to be deemed that by issuance of receipt, the DCT, or his authorized officer, is passing an order that the return submitted by an assessee is a correct return and that it is a complete return as submitted in accordance with the visions under sub-section (2) of Section 75, and that correct amount of tax has been paid in accordance with section 74 of the said Ordinance. 

 20. Thus, in addition to the creation of legal fiction by the Legislature, there are some others practical aspects through which the DCT, or his authorized officer, in fact passes an order by issuing receipt under sub-section (1) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance. Upon issuance of receipt, after such submission of correct and complete return by the assessee, the DCT, or his authorized officer, in fact endorses the return submitted by the assessee and, in such a situation, in so far as the question of invocation of jurisdiction under section 120 is concerned, if the IJCT or IACT finds any error in the said return submitted by the assessee which is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue, he is entitled to invoke jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance inasmuch as that the said return has been endorsed as correct, and complete return by the DCT by issuance of receipt. 

 21. Therefore, from both aspects, namely the aspect of legal fiction as well as practical endorsement of the return submitted by the assessee, it cannot be said that issuance of receipt by the DCT or his authorized officer; under sub-section (1) of section 82BB does not generate any order of assessment. Thus, the above aspect of such practical endorsement of the return submitted by the assessee having been clarified by her Ladyship Madam Justice Zinat Ara in the above referred Kamal Uddin's Case (unreported Writ Petition No. 1481 of 2014), we are in full agreement with the said decision. Therefore, our considered view is that, by issuance of receipt under sub-section (1) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance, the concerned DCT, or his authorized officer, passes an order in so far as the said practical aspect of correctness and completeness of the said return is concerned. At the same time, by virtue of the legal fiction as created by our Legislature by providing the words "shall be deemed to be an order of assessment" in sub-section (1) of section 82BB, the jurisdiction of IJCT or IACT under section 120 of the said Ordinance has been recognized. 

 23. Mr Mosharaf Hossain, learned advocate appearing for the petitioner, has not in fact made any submission on this point except that he supports the view on this point as adopted by the above referred two differently constituted Benches of this Court in Jamuna On  Case and Kamal Uddin's case. 

 24. However, Mr S Rashed Jahangir, learned DAG, submits that the preconditions under section 120 for invocation of jurisdiction being only two, namely that the order of the DCT has to be erroneous and that the said error is prejudicial to the revenue, the Court cannot read anything else therein which has not been provided by the Legislature in the said provision. Learned DAG further argues that, the concerned provisions being a fiscal provision, it has to be interpreted strictly as it is and no other qualification as regards such error in the order of the DCT can be read by the Court. 

 25. It appears from Jamuna Oil's Case (ITRA No. 29 of 2010) that, the said case was concerning invocation of jurisdiction under section 120 as against return submitted and receipt issued under section 83 of the said Ordinance in respect of return submitted by the assessee for assessment year 2003-2004. Therein, a Division Bench presided over by his Lordship Mr. Justice AFM Abdur Rahman, in addition to considering other issues as regards invocation of jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance, has held that such invocation of jurisdiction can only be done if the error in the order of the DCT is only an error of law and not an error of facts. In doing so, his Lordship (Justice Rahman) heavily relied on a decision of the Calcutta High Court in Al Jute Mills vs SK Dun, 1956 AIR, Calcutta 450. By quoting relevant paragraphs of the judgment delivered by his Lordship Mr Justice Sinha in the said AJ Jute Mill's case, the said Bench observed: 

 26. Again, though the above Calcutta High Court Case or any other authority was not specifically referred to in the judgment delivered by another Division Bench in Kamal Uddin's case (Writ Petition No. 1481 of 2014), which was a clear case of invoking jurisdiction under section 120 in respect of return under section 82 BB, the author Judge (Justice Zinat Ara), at one stage, observed: 

 "However, by now it is a settled principle of law that the IACT (Sic.) may invoke his jurisdiction under section 120 of the Ordinance only where the order passed by the DCT is erroneous in so far as it is prejudicial to the interest of the government revenue and the error of the DCT must be an error of law and not an error on facts. 

 28. To appreciate the submissions of the learned advocates as well as the views expressed by the said two differently constituted Benches of this courts let us first quote the relevant provisions under sub-section (1) of section 120 of the said Ordinance: 

 The Inspecting Joint Commissioner may call for from the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes 'and examine the record of any proceeding under this Ordinance, and, if he considers that any order passed therein by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is erroneous in so far as it is  prejudicial to the interests of the  revenue, he may, after giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard, and after making or causing to be made, such inquiry as he thinks necessary, pass such order thereon as in his view the circumstances of the case would justify, including an order enhancing or modifying the assessment or cancelling the assessment and directing a fresh assessment to be made, 

 ii) Such error in the order is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. 

 31. In this regard, we have carefully examined the above referred Calcutta High Court case in AI Jute Mills vs SK Dutt, 1956 AIR, Calcutta 450, as the said decision as well as the observations of Justice Sinha therein have been heavily relied upon by his Lordship Mr Justice Rahman in Jamuna Oil's Case. It appears that, in the said case, the assessee-petitioner invoked writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution challenging an order passed by the concerned Commissioner of Tax in exercise of similar power conferred on him under section 263 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 of India. In the said case, at one point, it was argued from the side of the Tax Department that the writ of certiorari was not maintainable inasmuch as that there was alternative remedy of appeal. To address this objection raised by the learned advocate Mr Meyer, representing the Tax authority, his Lordship Mr Justice Sinha made several observations of law (including the ones quoted by his Lordship Justice Rahman in the said Jamuna Oil's case) relying on the decisions in England, in particular the decision in Northumberland Compensation case, as regards the issue of maintaina1ility of writ of certiorari. Upon meticulous scrutiny of the said judgment of Justice Sinha in the said Al Jute Mills case, it appears that, invocation of revisional jurisdiction under similar provision of section 263 of the Indian Income Tax Act. 1961 was not an issue in that case at all. The only issue as against which Justice Sinha made such observation was whether against exercise of power and passing of an order by the Commissioner under section 263, the writ of certiorari could lie given that the statute had provided specific forum of appeal against such order after deduction of certain amount of tax to be payable by the assessee. In that context, Justice Sinha made the said observation as quoted by his Lordship Justice Rahma in the aforesaid judgment of Jamuna Oil's case. Therefore, we do not find any iota of indication in the said judgment of Calcutta High Court on the basis of which we can say that the jurisdiction under section 120 can be invoked only on error of law. Thus, under any circumstances, the said Calcutta High Court case cannot be relied upon as an authority to reach such a conclusion. We also do not find any reason as to why this decision of Calcutta High Court was so heavily relied upon by the said Division Bench in order to hold the view that the jurisdiction under section 120 can only be exercised on error of law and not on error of facts. We also fail to understand as to why another Division Bench presided over by her Ladyship Justice Zinat Ara, in Kamal Uddin's case also adopted the same view in that the error of the DCT must be an error of law and not an error of facts. 

 32. The authority on this is rather different. While examining the similar provision, namely section 263 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 of India and similar issues as regards pre-requisites for the exercise of revisional jurisdiction by the Commissioner under the said provision, the Indian Supreme Court, in Malabar Industrial Company Limited vs CIT, 243 ITR 83, held that the Commissioner has to be satisfied twin condition to invoke jurisdiction under the said provisions, namely that: i) The order of the assessing officer sought to be revised is erroneous, and ii) It is prejudicial to the interest of the Revenue. 

 33. It has been further held that the jurisdiction under section 120 cannot be invoked to correct each and every type of mistake or error committed by the assessing officer. It can only be invoked when such error is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue and in exercising such power the revising officer can correct both errors of fact and law and his jurisdiction is not restricted to correcting the errors of law alone.  Similarly, a Division Bench of the Elahabad High Court, in Jubilant Organosys vs CIT 265 ITR 420, held that the Commissioner under such jurisdiction can correct both errors of fact and errors of law and his jurisdiction is not restricted to correcting errors of law alone. Delivering the judgment for the Elehabad High Court in the said case, his Lordship Justice M Katju has observed as follows: "Before parting with this case we may mention that under section 263 of the Income Tax Act, the Commissioner of Income-tax can correct both errors of fact and errors of law. His jurisdiction is not limited to correcting errors of law alone as there is no such express restriction in the language of section 263.  The only requirement is that the impugned order should be prejudicial to the revenue. " 

 34. In view of the facts and circumstances of the instant writ petitions as well as the legal authorities referred to above, we are of the view that there is no such restriction under section 120 of the said Ordinance under which the IJCT or IACT can be restricted to correct the errors of law only in the order of the DCT. Since the Legislature has not provided any such restriction under section 120 and since in accordance with the settled principal of law, the Court does not Legislate, we are not in a position to read something else which is not in the said provisions under section 120 of the said Ordinance. Thus, we are of the view that, the IJCT or IACT can exercise jurisdiction under section 120 if the two conditions mentioned hereinabove the fulfilled, namely that the order passed by the DCT, or his authorized officer, is erroneous and that such error is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. Therefore, the IJCT or IACT is empowered under section 120 to exercise revisional jurisdiction in respect of error in the order of the DCT, irrespective of error of law or fact, if it is found that such error is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. 

 36. According to Mr Mosharaf, since the procedure for reopening an assessment or deemed assessment has been provided under sub-section (3) of section 82BB, which is a complete and comprehensive provision, reopening of return submitted under sub-section (1) of section 82 BB is not allowed under any other provisions of the said Ordinance. In this regard, learned advocate submits that, since the provision under sub-section (3) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance starts with a non-obstante clause, namely "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) and section 93", this non-obstante clause debars exercise of jurisdictions either under section 93 or under section 120 of the said Ordinance for reopening such deemed assessment completed upon issuance of receipt by the DCT after submission of return under Universal Self-Assessment Scheme. In this regard, he has put his entire weight on the decision of a Division Bench of this Court presided over by his Lordship Mr Justice Md Ashfaqul Islam in the above referred Abu Hena's Case. 

 37. As against above submissions, Mr S Rashed Jahangir, learned Deputy Attorney-General, submits that when a jurisdiction or exercise of jurisdiction under any particular provision is not clearly ousted by the statute, it cannot to be held to be ousted. In this regard, learned DAG has referred to the concerned Chapter in the books of Late Mr Mahmudul Islam, Interpretation of Statutes and Documents, Chapter-3 (Jurisdiction of regular Courts are not ousted except by express enactment or by necessary implication) and submits that, though the said Chapter deals with the issue regarding ouster of jurisdiction of Courts, same principle of law should be applied in the present scenario as the proceedings of the IJCT are deemed to be judicial proceedings in view of the provisions under section 122 of the said Ordinance and that he can exercise some powers vested in the Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 39. It appears from the decision of the said Division Bench of this Court in Abu Hena's Case, which was a case involving invocation of jurisdiction under section 93 as against return submitted under section 82BB (1), his Lordship Mr Justice Md Ashfaqul Islam has expressed the view that because of the reopening scheme as provided under sub-section (3) of section 82BB, return submitted under sub-section (1) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance and the consequent deemed assessment thereon can only be reopened in the manner as specified in sub-section (3) of section 82BB. Relevant paragraphs of the said decision in Abu Hena's Case are quoted below: 

 "17. If we glean these provisions and read them together, we find that when a return is filed by an assessee under section 82BB (1) that shall be deemed to be an order of assessment for a particular year. This provision is protected by sub-section (3) of the said section. That is to say that the privilege which has been given to an assessee under 82BB (1) cannot be misinterpreted on any pretext. For that reason section 82BB (3) restricts the right to reopen the return which has been filed under 82BB(1), it can only be reopened in the manner as specified in sub-section (3) of section 82BB that is only at the behest of the National Board of Revenue (NBR) it can be reopened. Where it is required by the Board that some returns filed under sub-section (I) of 82BB are to be sent to Deputy Commissioner of Taxes for the purpose of Audit only in that course of event assessment under section 83 or section 84 has been allowed. By any stretch of imagination it cannot be said that a return filed under section 82BB(I) can be reopened under section 93 of the Ordinance. 

 19. Section 82BB (3) has direct bearing upon the said interpretation and fortifies the same. Since the legislature intended to give a special privilege to an assessee founded upon trust, that cannot be curtailed by applying section 93 of the Ordinance when the legislature has categorically made provision for reopening the return filed under 82BB (1) by bringing sub-section (3) of section 82BB of the Ordinance which says that only for the purpose of Audit Deputy Commissioner Taxes can reopen the same at the behest of the National Board of Revenue. " 

 40. As stated above, though the above case was decided on the issue of invocation of jurisdiction under section 93 as against a return submitted under Universal Self Declaration Scheme, the said decision has direct bearing on the cases before us though here we are concerned with invocation of jurisdiction under section 120 as against similar return submitted under sub-section (1) of section 82BB. The reason for such bearing of the said decision is that, the said Division Bench in the said decision has held that sub-section (3) of section 82BB has given a protection to a return submitted under sub-section (1) of section 82BB and that sub-section (3) restricts the right to reopen the return which has been filed under section 82BB(1). Not only that, the said Division Bench has further held that, a return submitted under sub-section (1) of section 82BB can only be reopened in the manner as specified in sub-section (3) of section 82BB. This view, as expressed by the said Division Bench, has been heavily relied upon by the learned advocate for the petitioner who then has submitted that because of that view expressed by this Court, jurisdiction under section 120 as well cannot be invoked as against a return submitted sub-section (1) of section 82BB. Therefore, to decide the entire jurisdictional questions as raised by the petitioners in the instant two writ petitions, we need to adjudicate upon that issue as well. 

 41. It appears from sub-section (3) of section 82BB that, the said sub-section starts with a 'non-obstante clause', i.e. "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1)". It has been held repeatedly by the Superior Courts that a 'non-obstante clause' is provided at the beginning of a provision with a view to give the enacting part of the said provision, in case of conflict, an overriding effect over the provision or act mentioned in the non-obstante clause. [(See Union of India vs GM Kokil, 1984 (Supp) SCC 196)]. According to Justice GP Singh, Principles of Statutory Interpretation, 11th Edition, 2008 (Wadhwa and Nagpur), "Ordinarily, there is a close approximation between the non obstante clause and the enacting part of the section and the non obstante clause may throw some light as to the scope and ambit of the enacting part in case of its ambiguity, but when the enacting part is clear its scope cannot be cut down or enlarged by resort to non obstante clause. Further, the wide amplitude of a non obstante clause must be kept confined to the legislative policy and it can be given effect to, to the extent Parliament intended and not beyond the same ". 

 45. We also fail to understand as to how the provisions under sub-section (3) have any conflict with the provisions under section 120 of the said Ordinance. Therefore, while sub-section (3) of section 82BB has conferred a power on the NBR "notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1) to select some returns and send the same to the DCT for the purpose of audit etc., the provisions under section 120 has conferred revisional jurisdiction on the IJCT or IACT to correct any error in the order or deemed assessment order as passed of the DCT if such error is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. While vide sub-section (3) of section 82BB the Legislature has empowered the NBR to select some of the returns submitted under Universal Self-Assessment Scheme to send the same for assessment under sections 83 or 84, the Legislature has, at the same time, conferred jurisdiction on the IJCT or IACT to correct an error in the order or deemed assessment order of the DCT. Thus, apparently there being no conflict between the provisions under sub-section (3) and provisions under section 120 of the said Ordinance and the non obstante clause as occurring under sub-section (3) of the section 82BB having not even referred to the provisions under section 120, we fail to understand as to how this sub-section (3) of section 82BB has restricted the jurisdiction of IJCT or IACT under section 120 of the said Ordinance. This being so, for the sake of harmonious interpretation, this Court is of the view that, sub-section (3) of section 82BB, either by its non obstante clause or by any other provision therein, does not debar or restrict the invocation of jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance on a deemed assessment order passed by the DCT, or his authorized officer, upon issuance of receipt on a return submitted by an assessee under Universal Self-Assessment Scheme in view of the provisions under sub-section (1) of section 82BB. 

 46. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances of the case and discussions of relevant provisions of law as well as interpretation given by different superior Courts, our orders on the above referred three points of law are as follows: 

 1. The words "deemed to be an order of assessment" as occurring in sub-section (1) of section 82BB of the said Ordinance do generate an order of the DCT, or his authorized officer, upon issuance of a receipt after acceptance of a correct and complete return under Universal Self-Assessment Scheme in view of the provisions under section 82BB(1) of the said Ordinance. Therefore, the IJCT or 1ACT has an order of DCT before them to find error therein. 

 2. For invocation of jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance, the IJCT or IACT has to be satisfied of twine conditions, namely that: (i) the order of the DCT, or his authorized officer, is erroneous and (ii) that such error is prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. Thus, such jurisdiction under section 120 of the said Ordinance can be invoked to correct both errors of fact and law and that such jurisdiction is not restricted to correct the errors of law only. 

 48. Since the confusions as regards interpretations of law, in particular provisions under sections 82BB and 120 of the said Ordinance, have in fact been created by different conflicting judgments of this Court, we are of the view that, the petitioners in the instant writ petitions should be allowed to prefer Appeals, or Revisional Applications in accordance with law, in which case, the authorities concerned should take lenient view in considering the issue of condonation of delay.
